questions.q: `String a = "ACC"; String b = new String("ACC");` What do `a == b` and `a.equals(b)` return?
o: `false` and `true`
`true` and `true`
`false` and `false`
`true` and `false`
questions.w: `==` compares references, and `new String` creates a separate heap object. `equals` compares the characters.

questions.q: A method receives `String input` that may be `null`. Which comparison is safe?
o: `"ACC-1".equals(input)`
`input.equals("ACC-1")`
`input == "ACC-1"` for the pooled literal
`input.compareTo("ACC-1") == 0`
questions.w: Call `equals` on the known non-null literal, or use `Objects.equals`. The other forms throw or compare references.

questions.q: Why is building a 10,000-line report with `s = s + line` in a loop slow?
o: Each pass creates a new String and copies everything built so far
Strings are stored on disk until the loop completes
The `+` operator locks the string pool on every pass
Java converts each line to bytes before appending it
questions.w: That is O(n²) copying plus garbage. A `StringBuilder` appends in place and creates one String at the end.

questions.q: Which is NOT a reason why `String` is immutable?
o: It makes string concatenation faster than with a builder
It lets literals be shared safely in the string pool
It allows the hash code to be cached for map keys
It makes strings safe to share between threads
questions.w: Immutability actually makes repeated modification more expensive, which is why `StringBuilder` exists.

o: `true`: the compiler folds constants into the pooled literal
`false`: concatenation always creates a new object
`true`: `==` compares the characters of strings
It does not compile because `+` needs a variable
questions.w: Constant expressions are evaluated at compile time. With a non-final variable the concatenation happens at run time and gives a new object.

questions.q: `"a.b".split(".")` returns an empty array. What is the cause?
o: The argument is a regex where `.` matches any character
`split` only accepts single characters, not strings
The string has no whitespace to split on
`split` drops every part that has a punctuation mark
questions.w: Escape it: `split("\\.")`. `replace` takes literal text, while `replaceAll` and `split` take regular expressions.

questions.q: Which design step is required to make this class truly immutable? `class Statement { private final List<Entry> entries; Statement(List<Entry> e) { entries = e; } }`
o: Copy the list in the constructor, e.g. `List.copyOf(e)`
Declare the list field as `volatile` instead of final
Add a synchronized getter for the list field
Store the list in a static field of the class
questions.w: `final` only fixes the reference. A caller who keeps the original list can still change it, so make a defensive immutable copy.
